explanations.answer: The rock they were cut from
explanations.explanation: That's the picture, friend. The LORD says, “Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn.” Stone, cut out of a quarry. He's telling them to look back at where they came from.
A tree is a nice guess, and it's a picture a lot of folks would reach for. But the LORD says “…the rock from which you were cut…” Cut, not grown. Nothing leafy in this verse, just stone and a quarry.

explanations.answer: The clay they were shaped from
explanations.explanation: Clay is a fair guess, friend, since shaping pictures come up a lot. But the verse says, “Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn.” Cut and hewn are stone words, and a quarry is a place where stone is cut out. So the picture is rock, not clay.
Abraham it is. The LORD says, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth.” Notice he doesn't send them to Abraham alone. Sarah gets named right beside him, and I love that.

Moses is a big name, so I see why he jumped out. But he isn't in these verses. The LORD says, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth.” Sarah's name is the clue that points you to Abraham.

David is a famous name, and I get the pull. But the LORD doesn't mention him here. He says, “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth.” When a verse hands you a name right in it, friend, grab that one.
That's it. The LORD says, “…he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him.” One man became way more than one man. That's a big jump, and the LORD is the one who did it.

That's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “…he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him.” Blessed and multiplied is the opposite of being left to wander. One is where Abraham started, and the LORD took it from there.

explanations.answer: Made him king over the nations
explanations.explanation: King is a big title, but this verse never hands Abraham one. It says, “…he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him.” Blessed, and multiplied. Sometimes the text is simpler than we expect, and I'm okay with that.

Eden, yes. The verse says the LORD “…will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD.” Eden is where the LORD God planted a garden (Genesis 2:8). So Zion's dry, empty places get a whole garden picture.

Egypt is a real place name, so it sounds right at first. But the verse says the LORD will make her wilderness “like Eden.” The same verse goes on with “…her desert like the garden of the LORD.” That's where the picture is headed.

Sinai is another place name, and I see why it came to mind. But the verse names Eden: “He will make her wilderness like Eden…” The garden of the LORD comes right after it in the same line. Sinai isn't in this verse at all.

I get why that sounded right, since ruins can sound sad. But the verse goes the other way. It says, “Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and melodious song.” Mourning isn't what fills her streets.
False is right. The LORD will comfort Zion, and the verse says, “Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and melodious song.” That's the sound after the comfort. Singing, not mourning.

LAW, baker! The LORD says, “…a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations…” The law heads out the door, and His justice flips the lights on for the nations. That's the whole line, and it's a bright one.

An army would make a lot of noise, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “…a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations…” What goes out is a law. The light is His justice.

Famine is a heavy word, and it doesn't belong in this verse. The LORD says, “…a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations…” What goes out from Him is a law. And right after it comes a light, which is a lot nicer to picture.

True, and I LOVE how plain it is. The LORD lays out His law and His justice as a light to the nations. Then He says, “I will bring it about quickly.” No small print, no "terms and conditions apply." Just a promise, friend, and He means it.

I see why you'd pause, but the verse says otherwise. The LORD says His law will go out and His justice will become a light to the nations. Then He adds, “I will bring it about quickly.” So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: Look for Him and wait in hope
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The verse says, “The islands will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm.” Looking and waiting in hope. Far-off places are watching for Him.

explanations.answer: Hide from Him and turn away
explanations.explanation: Hiding would be the opposite of what the verse says. It says, “The islands will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm.” They look for Him, not away from Him. Hope is the mood here.

explanations.answer: Forget Him and go their way
explanations.explanation: Forgetting Him? Friend, that would be a plot twist, and this verse doesn't have one. The islands “…will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm.” That's far-off places with their eyes on the horizon, not wandering off. I think they're the folks who check the window every five minutes for good news.

Salvation, yes. The LORD says, “But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail.” The heavens vanish and the earth wears out, but His salvation stays put. That's a big comfort to hold onto.

Temple is a good guess, since it's a big, important building. But the verse doesn't say that. It says, “But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail.” What lasts is His salvation.

City is a fair guess, since Zion came up a few verses back. But this verse says, “But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail.” The word is salvation. His righteousness gets its own forever line, too.

explanations.answer: Moths will eat them like a garment
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool.” Moths and worms eat cloth, so the picture is easy to see. And right after it, His righteousness lasts forever.

explanations.answer: Their own insults will fall on them
explanations.explanation: That sounds neat, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool.” The picture is cloth and moths, not insults boomeranging. I'd stick with the verse.

explanations.answer: They will be scattered like dust
explanations.explanation: Dust is a good picture, but the verse doesn't use it here. It says, “For the moth will devour them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool.” A moth and a worm, working on cloth. Then comes the contrast: His righteousness will last forever.

explanations.answer: A road for the redeemed to cross over
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The speaker asks, “Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?” A road, right through the deep. The redeemed walked across.

explanations.answer: A home for the creatures of the deep
explanations.explanation: That's a fun idea, but the verse doesn't say it. The speaker says the LORD “…made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?” The road is for the redeemed to cross over, and that's the whole picture here.

explanations.answer: A wall to hold back the enemy
explanations.explanation: A wall would sound sturdy, and I see why you picked it. But the verse says the LORD “…made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?” The word is road, not wall. The point is crossing over.
Everlasting joy, yes. The verse says the redeemed “…will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy.” That's a crown I'd wear all day. Gladness and joy overtake them, too.
Gold and silver would shine, and crowns are usually fancy. But this crown is different. The verse says they enter Zion “…crowned with everlasting joy.” Joy is the crown.
Royal honor fits the crown picture, so I see the thinking. But the verse says they enter Zion “…crowned with everlasting joy.” The thing on their heads is joy. And it lasts forever.

I see why a heavy word like sorrow might stick around, but the verse says the opposite. It says, “Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.” Sorrow runs away. It doesn't follow anybody in.
False is right. The verse says, “Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.” Joy is the one catching up with them. Sorrow is the one running off.
Grass is right. The LORD says, “Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?” Grass turns brown and gives out. So why fear what withers?

Cedar is a tall, sturdy tree, and I see why it came to mind. But the verse says, “…a son of man who withers like grass?” Grass is the word, and it's a picture of something that withers. So why fear what withers?

Stone doesn't wither, friend. The LORD says, “Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?” Grass withers, and stone stays put. It's an easy one to mix up, because earlier verses had a rock in them.

Yes. The LORD says, “You live in terror all day long because of the fury of the oppressor who is bent on destruction.” It's a heavy picture of living afraid. And it comes right after they've forgotten their Maker.
That would be nice, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “You live in terror all day long because of the fury of the oppressor who is bent on destruction.” Terror is the word, not peace.

Pride is a good guess, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “You live in terror all day long because of the fury of the oppressor who is bent on destruction.” Fear is what's going on here, not boasting. I think it's a hard way to spend a day.
Freed is the word. The LORD says, “The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon, and his bread will not be lacking.” Out of the dungeon, not stuck in it. And it says soon.
Judged sounds official, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon…” The captive gets freed. That's good news for the one locked up.

I understand why a dungeon makes you think of that. But the verse says, “The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon…” Freed is the word the LORD uses. It's a promise, and it sounds like good news to me.
True. The verse ends with, “…and his bread will not be lacking.” Out of the dungeon, and not going hungry. The LORD covers both.

I get why you'd doubt it, since a dungeon doesn't sound like a place with plenty. But the LORD says, “The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon, and his bread will not be lacking.” So the statement is true.

That's the line. The LORD says, “I have put My words in your mouth, and covered you with the shadow of My hand…” and it ends with “…to say to Zion, ‘You are My people.’…” After all the promises, that's what He says to Zion. It's a warm place to land.

Rebuilding walls is a good guess, since Zion has ruins. But this verse never says that. It ends with the LORD saying to Zion, “You are My people.” That's the last word, and it's about who they belong to.
Waiting is a fair guess, since the passage talks about things on the way. But that's not what the LORD says to Zion at the end. He says, “You are My people.” Four words, and they land hard.
